attributes.title: Level 1

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ What keywords were used to add the 2 sprite kinds at the top of the editor?
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by noticing that 2 sprite kinds and several code comments have already been added at the top of the editor!

 

In the JavaScript editor, there are 4 pre-loaded sprite kinds: Player, Enemy, Projectile, and Food. Just like in the blocks editor, new sprite kinds can be added to a project to customize game play.

 

Notice the new keywords in blue: namespace and export. A namespace is a separate section of code inside curly brackets { }. The namespace will help organize code in a project, similar to code comments. However, the code inside the namespace’s block statement needs to be exported in order for it to be used in the rest of the project.

 

These new keywords are followed by let and the names of the 2 new sprite kinds: EnemyProjectile and PlayerProjectile. An assignment operator is used to create the sprite kinds using the SpriteKind.create() function.

 

Now, the 2 new sprite kinds have been declared and will be able to be used throughout the project.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set a background image for the project and use the dot operator . to start a screen effect?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Which background image shows a winter scene?

❓ Which screen effect might you use to customize the project?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that the background images do not always appear in order in the JavaScript editor gallery. This means that they may have to scroll further down to find a winter scene image.
steps.instructions:
Transform the project into a winter scene!

 

Open Scene, drag [set background image to (img)] under // set up. Select a winter scene background image from the gallery.

 

Open Scene, drag [start screen (effect) effect] under // set up. Use the default effect blizzard or the dot operator . to access the list of possible effects in the code completion tool.

 

Click ▶ to see a winter scene appear on screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update the Player sprite name in setPosition, moveSprite, and setStayInScreen?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What position might you set the Player sprite to, so that it appears on the bottom left side of the screen?

❓ What should you set the vx and vy parameters to in the moveSprite code so that the Player sprite is only able to move up and down?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja of the x-coordinate range (0-160) and y-coordinate range (0-120) when setting the Player sprite’s position. 

💡 Remind the ninja that the vx parameter sets how quickly a sprite will move left and right on the screen. The vy parameter sets how quickly a sprite will move up and down on the screen.
steps.instructions:
Add a Player sprite to the project!


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] underneath // Player sprite set up. Select a Player sprite image from the gallery or My Assets and update the sprite name. Use the default kind argument SpriteKind.Player.


Position the Player sprite on the bottom left side of the screen. Open Sprites again, drag [set (mySprite) position to x y] underneath the Player sprite code, and update the x and y parameters.


Move the Player sprite up and down the left side of the screen. Open Controller and drag [move (mySprite) with buttons] underneath the position code. Replace mySprite with the Player sprite’s name, then update the vx and vy parameters, so that the Player sprite is only able to move up and down.


Keep the Player sprite in screen. Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) stay in screen (true)] underneath the Player sprite movement code. Update the sprite name, and use the default argument true.


Click ▶ to move the Player sprite vertically on the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the sprite kind for the Enemy sprite in the sprite.create function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How do you change a sprite’s sprite kind in the JavaScript editor?

❓ Did you set the Enemy sprite’s position to the bottom right side of the screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Walk through the process of changing a sprite’s sprite kind in the JavaScript editor. In the sprite.create code, the ninja should delete .Player, retype the dot operator ., then select Enemy as the new sprite kind.

💡 Remind the ninja of the x-coordinate range (0-160) and y-coordinate range (0-120) when setting the Enemy sprite’s position.
steps.instructions:
Add an Enemy sprite to participate in the snowball fight!


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] underneath // Enemy sprite set up. Select an Enemy sprite image from the gallery or My Assets and update the sprite name. Change the kind parameter by deleting .Player then retyping the dot operator . and selecting Enemy from the list of properties.


Position the Enemy sprite on the bottom right side of the screen. Open Sprites, drag [set (mySprite) position to x y] underneath the Enemy sprite code, and update the x and y parameters. Use the same y-coordinate as the Player sprite, so that both sprites start in the same vertical position. 


Click ▶ to see an Enemy sprite appear on screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update all of the Player projectile’s parameters in the createProjectileFromSprite function so that a snowball is thrown from the Player sprite towards the Enemy sprite?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is creating a projectile from a sprite in the JavaScript editor similar and different than the Blocks editor?

❓ Why should positive values be used in the vx parameter of the createProjectileFromSprite code?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Just as in the blocks editor, the createProjectileFromSprite function offers the same parameters in JavaScript. Make sure the ninja has replaced mySprite with the Player sprite’s name, so that the projectile is sent from the Player sprite.

💡 The vx parameter should be a positive value, so that the projectile is sent from the Player sprite towards the Enemy sprite (moving left to right across the screen).
steps.instructions:
Code the Player sprite to throw a snowball!


Open Controller and drag [run code on (button) button (event)] underneath // projectile code, using the default property A and default event Pressed. 


Open Sprites and drag [projectile (img) from (mySprite) with vx (vx) vy (vy)] inside the curly brackets { } of the controller.A event. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:


let projectile = sprites.createProjectileFromSprite

(img` `, mySprite, 50, 50)


Since there will be 2 types of projectiles in this project, rename this projectile playerProjectile


The createProjectileFromSprite function takes 4 parameters: img, sprite, vx, and vy. Click the palette to select a snowball image from My Assets, then replace mySprite with the Player sprite’s name. Set the vx parameter to a random integer between 50 and 100, and set the vy parameter to 0, so that a snowball is thrown towards the Enemy sprite.


Click ▶ then press A to send a snowball from the Player sprite!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update all of the Enemy projectile’s parameters in the createProjectileFromSprite function so that a snowball is thrown from the Enemy sprite towards the Player sprite?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How might you edit the Enemy sprite’s snowball so that it looks different from the Player sprite’s?

❓ Why should negative values be used in the vx parameter of the createProjectileFromSprite code?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Make sure the ninja has replaced mySprite with the Enemy sprite’s name, so that the projectile is sent from the Enemy sprite.

💡 The vx parameter should be a negative value, so that the projectile is sent from the Enemy sprite towards the Player sprite (moving right to left across the screen).
steps.instructions:
Code the Enemy sprite to throw a snowball back at the Player sprite!


Open Game and drag [run code on game update every (period) ms] under the controller.A event. Replace 500 with a value that sets how frequently a snowball will be thrown at the Player sprite.


Open Sprites and drag [projectile (img) from (mySprite) with vx (vx) vy (vy)] inside the curly brackets { } of the onUpdateInterval loop. 


Rename this projectile enemyProjectile


Select a different snowball image from My Assets, but use the paint editor to change its appearance. Replace mySprite with the Enemy sprite’s name. Set the vx parameter to -50, and the vy parameter to 0, so that a snowball is thrown from the Enemy sprite towards the Player sprite.


Copy (Ctrl + C) the Enemy sprite’s position code and paste (Ctrl + V) it underneath the projectile code. Update the y-coordinate so that randint is used to randomly place the Enemy sprite in a new position. Now, the Enemy sprite will move to a random y-position once a snowball has been thrown.


Click ▶ to see the Enemy sprite throw snowballs at the Player sprite, then change position!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the sprite kind for the Player and Enemy projectile sprites with the setKind function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where were the 2 new sprite kinds declared in the code?

❓ How do you access new sprite kinds added to a project?

❓ Why might it be useful to have two different types of projectile sprite kinds?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that the new sprite kinds (playerProjectile and enemyProjectile) were declared at the top of the editor in the namespace. Because the keyword export was used, these sprite kinds are able to be used elsewhere in the project, outside of the namespace’s curly brackets { }

💡 Explain to the ninja that sprite kinds are accessed in the same way, regardless of whether they were added or are defaulted in the editor. The ninja can use the dot operator . to access the list of properties, and select a sprite kind.

💡 Because there are 2 different projectiles, using 2 different sprite kinds will be useful for creating unique overlap events between each sprite and their projectiles.
steps.instructions:
Change each projectile’s sprite kind to create unique overlap events!


Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) kind to (value)] inside the curly brackets { } of the controller.A event, underneath the projectile code. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

mySprite.setKind(SpriteKind.Player)

Replace mySprite with playerProjectile. Change the kind parameter by deleting .Player and retyping the dot operator .


Notice that the 2 new sprite kinds appear in the code completion tool. Select PlayerProjectile from the list of properties .


Follow the same steps to set the sprite kind of the Enemy sprite’s projectile. Drag [set (mySprite) kind to (value)] inside the curly brackets { } of the onUpdateInterval loop, then replace mySprite with enemyProjectile. Change the kind parameter by deleting .Player, retyping the dot operator . and selecting EnemyProjectile from the list of properties .


Now, each projectile is set to a different sprite kind, which will be used to create unique overlap events.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the kind parameter to PlayerProjectile and otherKind parameter to Enemy in the onOverlap event?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when a PlayerProjectile sprite overlaps the Enemy sprite?

❓ Did you use sprite in the destroy code?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When a PlayerProjectile sprite overlaps the Enemy sprite, the PlayerProjectile is destroyed.

💡 The handler parameter matches the order of the onOverlap event's first two parameters. This means that sprite will refer to the kind parameter's sprite kind and that otherSprite will refer to the otherKind parameter's sprite kind.
steps.instructions:
Code something to happen when the Player sprite’s projectile overlaps the Enemy sprite!


Open Sprites and drag [run code on (sprite) of kind (kind) overlaps (otherSprite) of kind (otherKind)] underneath // PlayerProjectile overlaps Enemy. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

sprites.onOverlap(SpriteKind.Player, SpriteKind.Player, function(sprite: Sprite, otherSprite: Sprite) { })

The onOverlap function takes 3 parameters: kind, otherKind, and handler. Update the kind parameter by deleting .Player, retyping the dot operator . and selecting PlayerProjectile from the list of properties . Follow the same steps to change the otherKind parameter to Enemy 


Open Sprites and drag [destroy (mySprite)] inside the curly brackets { } of the onOverlap event. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

sprites.destroy(mySprite)

﻿Replace mySprite with sprite, so that the projectile is destroyed after it overlaps the Enemy sprite. 


Click ▶ to see what happens when the Player sprite’s projectile overlaps the Enemy sprite.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the kind parameter to EnemyProjectile and otherKind parameter to Player in the onOverlap event?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the EnemyProjectile overlaps the Player sprite?

❓ Did you use sprite in the destroy code?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the EnemyProjectile overlaps the Player sprite, the EnemyProjectile will be destroyed.

💡 The handler parameter matches the order of the onOverlap event's first two parameters. This means that sprite will refer to the kind parameter's sprite kind and that otherSprite will refer to the otherKind parameter's sprite kind.
steps.instructions:
Code something to happen when the Enemy sprite’s projectile overlaps the Player sprite!


Open Sprites and drag [run code on (sprite) of kind (kind) overlaps (otherSprite) of kind (otherKind)] underneath // EnemyProjectile overlaps Player. 


Update the kind parameter to EnemyProjectile and the otherKind parameter to Player 


Open Sprites and drag [destroy (mySprite)] inside the curly brackets { } of the onOverlap event. Replace mySprite with sprite, so that the projectile is destroyed after it overlaps with the Player sprite. 


Click ▶ to see what happens when the Enemy sprite’s projectile overlaps the Player sprite.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add changeScoreBy inside the curly brackets { } of the PlayerProjectile/Enemy and EnemyProjectile/Player onOverlap events?
steps.instructions:
Assign each sprite a score to keep track of how many times their projectiles have overlapped the other sprite!


Open Info and drag [set (player) score to (0)] under // set up. Keep the default PlayerInfo property set to player1. 


Copy (Ctrl + C) the setScore code and paste (Ctrl + V) it on a blank line underneath. Update the PlayerInfo property to player2


Code each sprite to earn a point when their projectile overlaps the other sprite. Open Info again and drag [change (player) score by (1)] inside the onOverlap event underneath // PlayerProjectile overlaps Enemy. Keep the PlayerInfo property set to player1. 


Copy (Ctrl + C) the changeScoreBy code and paste (Ctrl + V) it inside the onOverlap event underneath // EnemyProjectile overlaps Player. Update the PlayerInfo property to player2 


Click ▶ to see each sprite score a point when their projectile overlaps the other sprite!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use an relational operator > to check if each sprite’s score is greater than a certain number of points?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Which condition needs to be true in order for the game to end in a win? Which condition needs to be true in order for the game to end in a loss?

❓ Did you drag info.player1.score() from the Multiplayer section of Info, then update the PlayerInfo property?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Walk through the logic of the code with the ninja. Throughout the project, if player1’s (Player sprite) score is greater than 5, then the game will end in a win. If player2’s (Enemy sprite) score is greater than 5, then the game will end in a loss. 

💡 Make sure that the ninja has selected the correct multiplayer functions for the score code. They should scroll all the way to the bottom of the Info category to access the Multiplayer functions.

💡 Instead of using the copy and paste keyboard shortcuts, the ninja can open Info again and replace true with [(player) score] inside the parentheses of the else if condition.
steps.instructions:
Code the game to end once one of the sprites earns a certain number of points!


Open Loops and drag [run code forever] underneath // game end. Open Logic and drag [if else] inside the curly brackets { } of the forever loop. Create an else if condition by typing if followed by parentheses ( ) next to the else keyword. 


Inside the parentheses of the if condition, delete true then open Info and replace it with [(player) score]. Keep the PlayerInfo property set to player1. Type a greater than relational operator > and a value that sets how many points each sprite needs to win the game. Copy (Ctrl + C) the code inside the parentheses of the if condition, then paste (Ctrl + V) it inside the parentheses of the else if condition. Update the PlayerInfo property to player2 


Finally, open Game and drag [game over (true)] inside the curly brackets of each condition. Set the game to end in a win if the Player sprite has earned the goal number of points and end in a loss if the Enemy sprite has earned the goal number of points. Be sure to add an effect parameter, too.


Click ▶ to see the game end when a sprite has earned a certain number of points!

steps.hints: ❓ What directions would help players understand how the game is played?
steps.instructions:
Finish the project by adding directions and sound effects!


Open Game and drag [splash (title)] underneath // set up. Update the title and subtitle parameters, so that a splash screen shares directions for the user to follow.


Open Music and drag [play (toPlay) (playbackMode)] inside the curly brackets { } of each onOverlap event. Use a dot operator . to select a sound to play from the code completion tool. 


Click ▶ to play the completed project!

subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses unique sprite kinds to make something happen when different types of sprites overlap.

validationItems.text: Set the background image and add a screen effect.
Use 1 Player sprite with a custom name, move it vertically with the controller, place it in the bottom left of the screen, and set it to stay in screen.
Use 1 Enemy sprite with a custom name and place it in the bottom right of the screen.
Create and launch a projectile when the player presses the A button. Set the projectile’s kind to PlayerProjectile.
Use an onUpdateInterval loop to make the enemy launch a projectile every few seconds.
Destroy the player projectile when it overlaps with the enemy sprite.
Destroy the enemy projectile when it overlaps with the player sprite.
Update player 1 and player 2 scores when the projectiles overlap the sprites.

attributes.description: Welcome to Level 1 of Purple Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about sprite kinds and sprite overlap events. In the JavaScript editor, you can use a namespace to create new sprite kinds. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 1:

badges.title: One of a Kind
badges.description: Use sprite kinds and events to control what happens to sprites in a project in JavaScript.

badges.title: A Meeting of the Kinds
badges.description: Use an overlap event that runs based on the sprites’ kinds.

badges.title: Nice Knowing Ya
badges.description: Write code that destroys a sprite.

badges.title: Life of the Party
badges.description: Set the value of the Player’s life.

badges.title: From One Sprite to Another
badges.description: Create a projectile that starts from the position of an existing sprite.

badges.title: Metamorphosis
badges.description: Change the sprite kind of an existing sprite.

badges.title: Kind of You to Join
badges.description: Create a new sprite kind in JavaScript.

badges.title: New Kind on the Block
badges.description: Write code that runs when a sprite with a specific sprite kind is created.

badges.title: Out of Chances
badges.description: Write code that runs when the Player’s life reaches zero.

badges.title: Spice Up Your Life
badges.description: Set the image used to represent the Player’s life.
